metadata.title: Overlearning is as ineffective as underlearning? A cross-culture study from PISA 2015

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PISA 2015 microdata for 15-year-old students from eight countries/regions and estimates multilevel models with schools as Level 2 and countries as Level 3. The manuscript does not report whether PISA sampling/student weights (and any replicate weights) were applied in Mplus, so weight usage cannot be confirmed from the text. For meta-analytic comparability, analysts should use the official PISA 2015 student/sampling weights when available in the dataset and apply the corresponding replicate-weight procedure if the software workflow supports it. Because the paper focuses on model fit and parameter estimates rather than PV-based prediction, the key weighting concern is representativeness across the complex sampling design (students nested in schools nested in countries).

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The dependent variable is the PISA 2015 science score used in multilevel regression, but the paper does not describe whether this score is treated as PV-based achievement with Rubin-style combining or as an IRT/WLE/scale score. Because the manuscript does not document the PV treatment and also does not report a missing-data strategy, this is a reporting gap that prevents verifying the exact psychometric handling. The authors also do not provide enough methodological detail to determine whether missing responses were excluded or imputed.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used PISA 2015 science learning time (smins) and science achievement for 15-year-old students from eight countries/regions (Japan, South Korea, Singapore, Chinese Taipei; and Canada, United Kingdom, Australia, United States). The analysis compares the full sample with a restricted subsample where standardized learning time is within ±3 SDs to reduce the influence of extremely long learning-time values. The paper does not report additional exclusions (e.g., missing ESCS/gender, school nonresponse) or any explicit missing-data rule.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2015 Grade 10/15-year-old Science (science learning time smins; science achievement score)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Multilevel model fit: quadratic vs linear models show smaller LL/AIC/BIC/aBIC in quadratic models across countries (Table 2). Parameter estimates (Model 1b full time): inverted U-shaped pattern with significant quadratic term β2 in all countries/regions (e.g., Australia β2=22.41***; United States β2=30.38***; Japan β2=21.12***; Singapore β2=36.53***). Optimal ztime (symmetry axis) for Model 1b full time: Australia 3.71; United States 4.98; United Kingdom 3.77; Canada 3.19; Chinese Taipei 4.16; Japan 0.84; South Korea 4.42; Singapore 3.51.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2015 Grade 10/15-year-old Science the study leveraged standardized science learning time (ztime), its squared term (ztime2), student gender, and socioeconomic status (ESCS) to model science achievement, finding an inverted U-shaped relationship where achievement increases up to an optimal learning-time point and then declines as learning time continues to rise. This indicates that policies should avoid “more time is always better” messaging and instead support guidance on achieving an optimal, sustainable amount of engaged science learning time.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2015 Grade 10/15-year-old Science (culture moderator; smins and science achievement)
main_findings.target_variable: Science achievement moderated by culture (east vs west)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Model 2a (full time) cultural interactive model: culture main effect β=38.79*** (d=0.50); culture×ztime β=14.30*; culture×ztime2 β=−1.89* (Table 4). Model 2a implied optimal ztime: East 3.85 vs West 3.92 (very similar symmetry axes). Model 2b (within ±3 SDs): culture×ztime2 β=−6.97*** (stronger moderation under restricted time range).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2015 Grade 10/15-year-old Science the study leveraged culture (east vs west) and its interactions with standardized learning time and squared learning time to model science achievement, finding that the optimal learning-time point is similar across cultures but the slope/steepness differs, with eastern students showing a more dramatic change in achievement as learning time moves away from the optimum. This indicates that curriculum and homework guidance should be culturally sensitive, emphasizing sustainable learning intensity to prevent overlearning-related declines, especially in East Asian contexts.

data.outcome_summary: This study analyzes PISA 2015 science data for 15-year-old students from eight countries/regions (N=75,404) to examine how engaged science learning time (smins, standardized as ztime) relates to science achievement. Using multilevel modeling with schools nested within countries, the authors compare linear and quadratic specifications and find that quadratic models fit better (lower LL/AIC/BIC/aBIC) and yield an inverted U-shaped pattern: science achievement rises with learning time up to an optimal point and then declines. The optimal ztime differs by country/region (e.g., Japan 0.84 vs South Korea 4.42 in the full-time model). A culture interaction model (east vs west) shows similar symmetry axes (optimal ztime ~3.85 East vs ~3.92 West) but stronger moderation in the eastern group, with steeper changes after the peak. Limitations include the absence of reported PV and missing-data handling details and no explicit discussion of survey-weight application.
